name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q01 - WHO definition of reproductive health

questiontext.text: According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), reproductive health means a total well-being in which of the following aspects of reproduction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reproductive health is not limited merely to the physical structure and normal functioning of reproductive organs; it encompasses a broader perspective involving emotional and social dimensions as well.

Step 2: Evaluation of the WHO Definition
The World Health Organisation (WHO) defines reproductive health as a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction, specifically physical, emotional, behavioural, and social.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A society whose members have physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects is considered reproductively healthy. Thus, the four aspects specified by WHO are physical, emotional, behavioural, and social.

answer.text: Physical, emotional, behavioural, and social
Physical, anatomical, hormonal, and genetic
Physiological, economic, educational, and political
Anatomical, clinical, cultural, and nutritional

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q02 - Initiation of family planning programmes in India

questiontext.text: India was amongst the first countries in the world to initiate national-level action plans and programmes called 'family planning' to attain total reproductive health as a social goal in the year:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
National-level reproductive health programmes in India began with family planning initiatives and were later expanded into Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

Step 2: Historical Milestone
India initiated its national-level 'family planning' programmes in 1951, making it one of the earliest countries to adopt reproductive health as a social goal.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The year of initiation of family planning programmes in India is 1951.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q03 - Purpose and statutory ban on amniocentesis

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the legitimate medical use of amniocentesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique in which a small sample of amniotic fluid surrounding the developing foetus is withdrawn for analysis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Diagnostic Purpose
The foetal cells and dissolved substances in the amniotic fluid are analysed to test for genetic disorders such as Down syndrome, haemophilia, and sickle-cell anaemia, and to determine the survivability of the foetus.

Step 3: Elimination of Misuses and Final Conclusion
Using amniocentesis for foetal sex-determination is statutorily banned in India to prevent female foeticide, and it is not used to treat infertility or administer vaccines. Therefore, its legitimate medical use is to test for genetic disorders and determine foetal survivability.

answer.text: Determining the sex of the foetus to assist couples in family planning
Analysing foetal cells and dissolved substances in amniotic fluid to detect genetic disorders such as Down syndrome, haemophilia, and sickle-cell anaemia
Transferring early embryos with up to 8 blastomeres into the fallopian tube
Administering immunisation doses directly into the amniotic sac before parturition

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q04 - Development of Saheli oral contraceptive at CDRI

questiontext.text: 'Saheli', a new oral contraceptive for females, was developed by scientists at which Indian research institute?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Research in reproduction-related areas is supported by governmental and non-governmental agencies in India to develop improved and safer contraceptive methods.

Step 2: Identification of the Institute
'Saheli' was developed by scientists at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) located in Lucknow, India.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the institute responsible for developing Saheli is the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

answer.text: All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi
National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), New Delhi
Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q05 - Role of sex education in schools

questiontext.text: Why should the introduction of sex education in schools be encouraged?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Creating awareness among adolescents and young individuals is a primary task under Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Purpose
Encouraging sex education in schools provides accurate information to young people, discouraging them from believing in myths and having misconceptions about sex-related aspects, while educating them about reproductive organs, adolescence, safe sexual practices, STDs, and AIDS.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The primary objective of school sex education is to provide right information to the young and dispel myths and misconceptions about sex-related matters.

answer.text: To provide right information to the young and discourage them from believing in myths and misconceptions about sex-related aspects
To replace the role of parents, teachers, and medical professionals in family planning
To promote surgical sterilisation as the primary contraceptive method among adolescents
To encourage early marriage before the statutory age limits

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q06 - Indicators of improved reproductive health in society

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of observations collectively indicates improved reproductive health of a society?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Improved reproductive health in a society is reflected by better awareness, enhanced medical infrastructure, and reduced maternal and infant mortality.

Step 2: Evaluation of Indicators
Key indicators of improved reproductive health include better awareness about sex-related matters, an increased number of medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care leading to decreased maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR), an increased number of couples with small families, better detection and cure of STDs, and overall increased medical facilities for sex-related problems.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Decreased MMR and IMR alongside increased medically assisted deliveries, better STD detection and cure, and wider adoption of small families indicate improved reproductive health.

answer.text: Increased maternal mortality rate, decreased medically assisted deliveries, and higher incidence of STDs
Increased infant mortality rate, widespread sex-selective amniocentesis, and larger family sizes
Decreased maternal and infant mortality rates, increased medically assisted deliveries, and better detection and cure of STDs
Increased illegal abortions by unqualified quacks and reduced post-natal care facilities

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q07 - World and Indian population growth figures

questiontext.text: According to demographic records, the world population and India's population in 2011 were approximately:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Improved health facilities and better living conditions in the last century caused an explosive growth in both world and Indian populations.

Step 2: Recall of Demographic Figures
The world population rose from about 2 billion in 1900 to 6 billion in 2000 and reached 7.2 billion in 2011. In India, the population grew from roughly 350 million at independence to close to 1 billion by 2000, and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, in 2011, the world population was 7.2 billion and India's population crossed 1.2 billion.

answer.text: 6.0 billion and 350 million
7.2 billion and over 1.2 billion
2.0 billion and 1.0 billion
8.5 billion and 1.5 billion

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q08 - Probable reasons for rapid population growth

questiontext.text: Which combination of factors best accounts for the rapid population explosion observed in India, and what was the population growth rate reported in the 2011 census?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Population growth accelerates when mortality rates decline rapidly while a large proportion of the population is in the reproductive age group.

Step 2: Evaluation of Causes and Census Data
Probable reasons for India's rapid population growth include a rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR), and infant mortality rate (IMR), along with an increase in the number of people in reproducible age. According to the 2011 census report, the population growth rate was less than 2 per cent, i.e., 20/1000/year.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A rapid decline in death rate, MMR, and IMR combined with more individuals in the reproducible age group drove the growth, with a 2011 census growth rate of less than 2 per cent.

answer.text: Increase in death rate and MMR; growth rate of 5 per cent
Decline in number of people in reproducible age; growth rate of 10 per cent
Increase in IMR and decline in medical facilities; growth rate of 4 per cent
Rapid decline in death rate, MMR, and IMR, plus more people in reproducible age; growth rate less than 2 per cent

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q09 - Statutory marriageable age in India

questiontext.text: To tackle uncontrolled population growth, the statutory marriageable age in India was raised to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alongside promoting contraceptives and small family norms such as 'Hum Do Hamare Do', statutory measures were enacted to delay marriage and childbirth.

Step 2: Recall of Statutory Limits
The statutory marriageable age in India was raised to 18 years for females and 21 years for males.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the minimum legal marriageable age is 18 years for females and 21 years for males.

answer.text: 18 years for females and 21 years for males
21 years for females and 18 years for males
16 years for females and 18 years for males
20 years for females and 25 years for males

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q10 - Characteristics of an ideal contraceptive

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of an ideal contraceptive?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An ideal contraceptive is designed to prevent unwanted pregnancy safely and acceptably without disrupting normal sexual function or long-term fertility.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ideal Properties
An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective, and reversible with no or least side-effects. Crucially, it should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire, and/or the sexual act of the user.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An ideal contraceptive must NOT interfere with the sexual drive, desire, or sexual act of the user; claiming that it should suppress sexual drive is incorrect.

answer.text: It should be user-friendly and easily available.
It should be effective and reversible with no or least side-effects.
It should reduce the sexual drive and desire of the user.
It should not interfere with the sexual act of the user.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q11 - Fertile period in periodic abstinence method

questiontext.text: In the periodic abstinence method of natural contraception, couples avoid coitus during which days of the menstrual cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Natural contraceptive methods work by avoiding the chances of ovum and sperms meeting without using medicines or devices.

Step 2: Identification of the Fertile Period
In periodic abstinence, couples abstain from coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected and chances of fertilisation are very high (hence called the fertile period).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, coitus is avoided from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle.

answer.text: Day 1 to 5
Day 10 to 17
Day 21 to 28
Day 5 to 9

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q12 - Mechanism of coitus interruptus

questiontext.text: How does the withdrawal (coitus interruptus) method prevent conception?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Withdrawal or coitus interruptus is a natural contraceptive method aimed at preventing the physical meeting of ovum and sperms.

Step 2: Mechanism
In this method, the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation so as to avoid insemination (deposition of semen into the female reproductive tract).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
By withdrawing before ejaculation, insemination is avoided, thereby preventing conception.

answer.text: By suppressing ovulation during intense lactation
By increasing phagocytosis of sperms inside the uterus
By thickening cervical mucus with progestogens
By withdrawing the penis from the vagina just before ejaculation to avoid insemination

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q13 - Lactational amenorrhea effectiveness and failure rate

questiontext.text: A mother who delivered a baby two months ago is breast-feeding the child fully and has not resumed menstruation. Which statement accurately describes her contraceptive status under the lactational amenorrhea method?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lactational amenorrhea (absence of menstruation) relies on the physiological fact that ovulation and the menstrual cycle do not occur during intense lactation following parturition.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conditions and Limits
As long as the mother breast-feeds the child fully, chances of conception are almost nil, and since no medicines or devices are used, side effects are almost nil. However, this method is effective only up to a maximum period of six months following parturition, and natural methods in general carry high chances of failure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
At two months post-parturition with full breast-feeding, chances of conception are almost nil, though the method remains effective only up to a maximum of six months following parturition.

answer.text: Chances of conception are almost nil while breast-feeding fully, but the method is effective only up to a maximum of six months following parturition.
It provides permanent contraception with zero chance of failure as long as lactation continues beyond one year.
It works by releasing copper ions that suppress sperm motility during the first six months.
Ovulation continues normally during intense lactation, but implantation is blocked by high estrogen levels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q14 - Additional benefit of using condoms

questiontext.text: Why has the use of condoms increased in recent years compared to other barrier methods?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Condoms are barrier methods made of thin rubber/latex sheath used to cover the penis in males or the vagina and cervix in females just before coitus.

Step 2: Evaluation of Additional Benefit
In addition to preventing conception by stopping ejaculated semen from entering the female reproductive tract, condoms offer the major additional benefit of protecting the user from contracting sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and AIDS. Both male and female condoms are disposable and self-inserted, providing privacy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The additional benefit of protection against STIs and AIDS has driven the increased use of condoms in recent years.

answer.text: They are reusable and can be left inside the uterus for several years.
They inhibit ovulation by releasing small doses of progestogens.
They provide the additional benefit of protecting the user from contracting STIs and AIDS.
They must be inserted by qualified doctors or expert nurses.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q15 - Reusable female barrier contraceptives and spermicides

questiontext.text: Diaphragms, cervical caps, and vaults are reusable rubber barriers inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus. What is commonly used along with these barriers to increase their contraceptive efficiency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Diaphragms, cervical caps, and vaults prevent conception by physically blocking the entry of sperms through the cervix.

Step 2: Enhancing Contraceptive Efficiency
Spermicidal creams, jellies, and foams are usually used along with diaphragms, cervical caps, and vaults to increase their contraceptive efficiency.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, spermicidal creams, jellies, and foams are used alongside these reusable cervical barriers.

answer.text: Non-steroidal oral tablets
Spermicidal creams, jellies, and foams
Copper-releasing intrauterine rods
Subdermal progestogen implants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q16 - Classification of intrauterine devices

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly classifies the given Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs) into non-medicated, copper-releasing, and hormone-releasing categories respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs) are available in three main categories: non-medicated IUDs, copper-releasing IUDs, and hormone-releasing IUDs.

Step 2: Categorisation of Examples
Lippes loop is a non-medicated IUD. CuT, Cu7, and Multiload 375 are copper-releasing IUDs. Progestasert and LNG-20 are hormone-releasing IUDs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Lippes loop (non-medicated), Cu7 (copper-releasing), and LNG-20 (hormone-releasing) represent the three categories in the respective order.

answer.text: CuT, Lippes loop, Progestasert
Progestasert, Multiload 375, Lippes loop
LNG-20, CuT, Multiload 375
Lippes loop, Cu7, LNG-20

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q17 - Contraceptive mechanisms of hormone-releasing IUDs

questiontext.text: In addition to increasing phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus, what additional contraceptive actions are exhibited by hormone-releasing IUDs such as Progestasert and LNG-20?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus, while medicated IUDs add specific chemical or hormonal effects.

Step 2: Comparison of Medicated IUDs
Copper-releasing IUDs release Cu ions that suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. In contrast, hormone-releasing IUDs (Progestasert, LNG-20) additionally make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and render the cervix hostile to sperms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.

answer.text: They make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.
They release copper ions that permanently destroy ovarian follicles.
They physically seal the fallopian tubes to block ovum transport permanently.
They prevent ejaculation by blocking the vas deferens.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q18 - Administration schedule of oral contraceptive pills

questiontext.text: How are conventional oral contraceptive pills containing small doses of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations administered?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oral pills contain small doses of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations that inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus quality.

Step 2: Administration Schedule
These pills are taken daily for a period of 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle. After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs), the 21-day cycle is repeated in the same pattern for as long as contraception is desired.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, conventional oral pills are taken daily for 21 days starting within the first five days of the menstrual cycle, followed by a 7-day gap.

answer.text: Once a week throughout the year without any gap
Daily for 7 days starting on day 14 of the menstrual cycle, followed by a 21-day gap
Daily for 21 days starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle, followed by a 7-day gap
Only as a single dose within 72 hours after ovulation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q19 - Distinguishing features of Saheli oral contraceptive

questiontext.text: Which set of features distinguishes 'Saheli' from conventional daily oral contraceptive pills?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conventional oral contraceptive pills contain steroidal hormones (progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations) and must be taken daily for 21 days.

Step 2: Comparison with Saheli
Saheli is a new oral contraceptive for females that contains a non-steroidal preparation. It is taken as a 'once a week' pill and offers very few side effects along with high contraceptive value.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Saheli is distinguished by being a non-steroidal, once-a-week pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value.

answer.text: Contains high-dose estrogen and progestogen; taken daily for 21 days
Contains a non-steroidal preparation; taken once a week with very few side effects and high contraceptive value
Inserted into the uterus by a doctor; releases copper ions to suppress sperm motility
Implanted under the skin; effective only for 72 hours after coitus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q20 - Emergency contraception window and methods

questiontext.text: To avoid possible pregnancy due to rape or casual unprotected intercourse, which emergency contraceptive measures are effective when administered within 72 hours of coitus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Emergency contraceptives are post-coital interventions used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or sexual assault before implantation occurs.

Step 2: Evaluation of Valid Emergency Methods
Administration of progestogens, progestogen-estrogen combinations, or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus has been found to be very effective as emergency contraceptives. Natural methods like periodic abstinence, barrier methods like condoms, or terminal surgical methods are not emergency post-coital contraceptives.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Progestogens, progestogen-estrogen combinations, or IUDs administered within 72 hours of coitus are effective emergency contraceptives.

answer.text: Periodic abstinence or coitus interruptus
Diaphragms or spermicidal foams
Vasectomy or tubectomy
Progestogens, progestogen-estrogen combinations, or IUDs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q21 - Definition and global scale of MTP

questiontext.text: Approximately how many Medical Terminations of Pregnancy (MTPs) are performed in a year all over the world, and what fraction of total conceived pregnancies do they represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is termed medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion.

Step 2: Recall of Global Figures
Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year worldwide, which accounts for 1/5th of the total number of conceived pregnancies in a year.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The global annual figure is 45 to 50 million MTPs, representing 1/5th of total conceived pregnancies.

answer.text: 45 to 50 million; 1/5th of total conceived pregnancies
10 to 15 million; 1/10th of total conceived pregnancies
80 to 90 million; 1/2 of total conceived pregnancies
20 to 25 million; 1/4th of total conceived pregnancies

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q22 - Legalisation of MTP in India with strict conditions

questiontext.text: The Government of India legalised Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) in 1971 with strict conditions primarily to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
MTP is performed to terminate unwanted pregnancies resulting from casual unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, or rape, or when continuing pregnancy is harmful or fatal to the mother or foetus.

Step 2: Rationale for Strict Legal Conditions
When India legalised MTP in 1971, strict conditions were imposed to prevent its misuse, especially to check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticides following sex-determination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Strict conditions were attached to the 1971 legalisation of MTP to avoid its misuse and check illegal female foeticides.

answer.text: Replace contraceptive methods as a routine population control measure
Allow unqualified practitioners to perform second-trimester abortions
Avoid misuse of MTP and check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticides
Encourage sex-determination of the unborn child through amniocentesis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q23 - Safe period for performing MTP

questiontext.text: Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) is considered relatively safe up to which stage of pregnancy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The medical risk associated with induced abortion increases significantly as gestation advances.

Step 2: Evaluation of Trimester Safety
MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester, i.e., up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, whereas second trimester abortions are much riskier.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, MTP is relatively safe during the first trimester (up to 12 weeks of pregnancy).

answer.text: Second trimester, up to 24 weeks
First trimester, up to 12 weeks
Third trimester, up to 36 weeks
Only between 18 and 24 weeks

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q24 - Medical practitioner opinion under MTP Amendment Act 2017

questiontext.text: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2017, what medical opinion is required to terminate a pregnancy that has lasted more than 12 weeks but fewer than 24 weeks?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2017 was enacted by the Government of India to reduce illegal abortions and consequent maternal mortality and morbidity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statutory Requirements
Within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, termination requires the opinion of one registered medical practitioner. However, if the pregnancy has lasted more than 12 weeks but fewer than 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners must be of the opinion, formed in good faith, that the required grounds exist.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Termination between 12 and 24 weeks requires the good-faith opinion of two registered medical practitioners.

answer.text: Opinion of one registered medical practitioner only
Opinion of any qualified nurse or midwife
No medical opinion is required if the woman consents
Opinion of two registered medical practitioners formed in good faith

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q25 - Valid grounds under MTP Amendment Act 2017

questiontext.text: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2017, which of the following is a valid legal ground for terminating a pregnancy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017 specifies strict medical and humanitarian grounds under which a pregnancy may be legally terminated.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statutory Grounds
The Act permits termination if: (i) continuation of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman or of grave injury to her physical or mental health; or (ii) there is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from such physical or mental abnormalities as to be seriously handicapped. Foetal sex preference or normal pregnancy discomfort are not valid grounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Substantial risk of serious physical or mental abnormalities causing the child to be seriously handicapped is a valid statutory ground for MTP.

answer.text: Substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities
Determination through amniocentesis that the developing foetus is female
Desire to avoid normal morning sickness during a healthy pregnancy
Preference for a male child after having two daughters

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q26 - Common sexually transmitted infections

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups consists exclusively of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Infections transmitted through sexual intercourse are collectively termed sexually transmitted infections (STIs), venereal diseases (VD), or reproductive tract infections (RTIs).

Step 2: Identification of Common STIs
Common STIs include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, and HIV leading to AIDS. Conditions such as Down syndrome, haemophilia, and sickle-cell anaemia are genetic disorders, not STIs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, and trichomoniasis are all sexually transmitted infections.

answer.text: Gonorrhoea, haemophilia, syphilis, and AIDS
Gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, and trichomoniasis
Genital herpes, Down syndrome, hepatitis-B, and genital warts
Syphilis, sickle-cell anaemia, chlamydiasis, and trichomoniasis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q27 - Non-sexual transmission of Hepatitis-B and HIV

questiontext.text: Besides sexual intercourse, infections such as hepatitis-B and HIV can also be transmitted through:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain STIs like hepatitis-B and HIV are transmitted not only via sexual contact but also through blood and body fluid exposure or vertical transmission.

Step 2: Evaluation of Non-Sexual Routes
Hepatitis-B and HIV can be transmitted by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments with infected persons, through transfusion of infected blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sharing injection needles or surgical instruments, blood transfusion, and transmission from an infected mother to the foetus are all recognised non-sexual routes for hepatitis-B and HIV.

answer.text: Sharing food and drinking water with an infected person
Casual handshakes and mosquito bites
Droplet inhalation from coughing or sneezing
Sharing injection needles or surgical instruments, blood transfusion, or from an infected mother to the foetus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q28 - Curability of sexually transmitted infections

questiontext.text: Which of the following combinations lists ONLY those sexually transmitted infections that are NOT completely curable even if detected early?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Most bacterial and protozoan STIs can be completely cured with timely diagnosis and proper treatment, whereas certain viral STIs remain incurable.

Step 2: Identification of Incurable STIs
Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes, and HIV infections, other common STIs (such as gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, and trichomoniasis) are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hepatitis-B, genital herpes, and HIV infections are the three STIs noted as not completely curable.

answer.text: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, and chlamydiasis
Trichomoniasis, genital warts, and syphilis
Hepatitis-B, genital herpes, and HIV
Chlamydiasis, gonorrhoea, and HIV

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q29 - Late complications of untreated STIs

questiontext.text: Lack of significant early symptoms and social stigma often deter infected individuals from seeking timely treatment for STIs. Which of the following complications can result later from untreated STIs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early symptoms of STIs are minor (itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings in the genital region) and infected females may often be asymptomatic, leading to delayed diagnosis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Late Complications
Untreated STIs can progress to severe complications including pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility, or even cancer of the reproductive tract.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancies, infertility, abortions, still births, and reproductive tract cancer are potential late complications of untreated STIs.

answer.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancies, infertility, and reproductive tract cancer
Down syndrome, haemophilia, and sickle-cell anaemia
Lactational amenorrhea and premature ovulation
Breakthrough bleeding and decreased sperm phagocytosis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q30 - High incidence age group and prevention of STIs

questiontext.text: Incidences of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) are reported to be very high among individuals in which age group, and what simple preventive measure helps protect against them during coitus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although all individuals are vulnerable to STIs, epidemiological data highlight a particularly high-incidence age group and straightforward preventive practices.

Step 2: Identification of Age Group and Prevention
The incidence of STIs is reported to be very high among persons in the age group of 15–24 years. Simple preventive principles include avoiding sex with unknown/multiple partners, always trying to use condoms during coitus, and consulting a qualified doctor early in case of doubt.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The high-incidence age group is 15–24 years, and using condoms during coitus helps prevent STI transmission.

answer.text: 5–14 years; using oral contraceptive pills
15–24 years; using condoms during coitus
35–44 years; using copper-releasing IUDs
45–54 years; using cervical caps with spermicides

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q31 - Definition and causes of infertility

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about infertility is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Infertility is defined as the inability to conceive or produce children even after 2 years of unprotected sexual cohabitation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Causes
The reasons for infertility can be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological, or even psychological. Although the female is often blamed in India for a couple being childless, more often than not the problem lies in the male partner.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Infertility has diverse causes—physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological, or psychological—and frequently involves the male partner rather than being solely a female defect.

answer.text: It is always caused by anatomical defects in the female partner.
It is diagnosed after just two months of unprotected sexual cohabitation.
It arises solely from genetic disorders and never from psychological or immunological factors.
It can result from physical, congenital, disease, drug, immunological, or psychological factors, and often lies in the male partner.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q32 - Embryo transfer site in ZIFT and IUT

questiontext.text: In the 'test tube baby' programme (IVF-ET), an early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the ______, whereas an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer (IVF-ET) involves forming a zygote under simulated laboratory conditions and transferring the resulting embryo at an appropriate developmental stage.

Step 2: Distinction Between ZIFT and IUT
A zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube (Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer, ZIFT). An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred directly into the uterus (Intra Uterine Transfer, IUT) to complete its further development.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct transfer sites are the fallopian tube (up to 8 blastomeres) and the uterus (more than 8 blastomeres).

answer.text: uterus; fallopian tube
vagina; cervix
fallopian tube; uterus
cervix; fallopian tube

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q33 - Application of Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer

questiontext.text: A woman cannot produce an ovum, but her reproductive tract can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further embryonic development. Which Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) is specifically suited for her?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different ART procedures address specific causes of male or female infertility, such as inability to produce ova, inability to conceive, or low sperm count.

Step 2: Matching Condition to Technique
Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer (GIFT) involves the transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce one, but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer (GIFT) is the specific ART procedure indicated in this scenario.

answer.text: Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer (GIFT)
Intra Cytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI)
Artificial Insemination (AI)
Tubectomy

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q34 - Artificial insemination and intra-uterine insemination

questiontext.text: Infertility cases due to the inability of the male partner to inseminate the female or due to very low sperm counts in the ejaculates can be corrected by which technique?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When male infertility is caused by inability to inseminate or very low sperm counts in the ejaculates, semen can be introduced artificially into the female genital tract.

Step 2: Identification of Technique
In the artificial insemination (AI) technique, semen collected either from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced either into the vagina or into the uterus (Intra-Uterine Insemination, IUI) of the female.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Artificial insemination (AI), including intra-uterine insemination (IUI), is used to correct infertility caused by inability to inseminate or very low sperm counts.

answer.text: Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer (GIFT)
Artificial Insemination (AI) / Intra-Uterine Insemination (IUI)
Amniocentesis
Vasectomy

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q35 - Limitations of ART and legal adoption in India

questiontext.text: Why are the benefits of Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART) currently affordable to only a limited number of people in India, and what legal alternative is highlighted for couples seeking parenthood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although ART offers multiple options for infertile couples, practical, financial, and socio-cultural barriers limit its widespread accessibility.

Step 2: Evaluation of Limitations and Alternative
ART techniques require extremely high precision handling by specialised professionals and expensive instrumentation, so facilities are available at only a few centres and remain affordable to a limited number of people. Emotional, religious, and social factors also act as deterrents. Given the large number of orphaned and destitute children in India, legal adoption is permitted by Indian laws and remains one of the best methods for couples looking for parenthood.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ART is limited by the need for specialised professionals, expensive instrumentation, and few centres, while legal adoption of orphaned and destitute children is highlighted as one of the best alternatives.

answer.text: ART is banned by Indian law; surrogacy is the only legal alternative.
ART requires no specialised training, but is avoided due to low success rates; surgical sterilisation is recommended instead.
ART is limited only to rural clinics; amniocentesis is recommended for parenthood.
ART requires high-precision handling by specialised professionals and expensive instrumentation at few centres; legal adoption is one of the best methods.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIVE_HEALTH_MCQ_Q36 - Why removal of gonads is not a contraceptive option

questiontext.text: Why can the surgical removal of gonads (testes or ovaries) NOT be considered a contraceptive option?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An ideal contraceptive should be reversible with no or least side effects and must not interfere with sexual drive, desire, or normal physiological well-being.

Step 2: Physiological Analysis of Gonad Removal
Gonads (testes and ovaries) are responsible not only for gamete production (spermatogenesis and oogenesis) but also for secreting essential sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen, progesterone) that regulate secondary sexual characters, sexual drive, and normal reproductive and metabolic physiology. Removing gonads causes permanent, irreversible sterility and severe hormonal deficiency, unlike vasectomy or tubectomy which only block gamete transport.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Removal of gonads leads to permanent, irreversible infertility and eliminates essential sex hormone production, interfering with sexual drive and normal physiology, so it cannot be considered a contraceptive option.

answer.text: Because gonads do not participate in gamete formation.
Because removal of gonads only blocks gamete transport temporarily.
Because it causes irreversible sterility and stops essential sex hormone secretion, severely affecting normal physiology and sexual drive.
Because gonads are located outside the reproductive tract and cannot be accessed surgically.
